faq.q: Does decoding a JWT prove it is genuine?
faq.a: No. The header and payload are only Base64URL-encoded, not encrypted, so anyone can read and even forge them. Decoding shows what a token claims; it says nothing about whether those claims were really issued by the server. To prove authenticity you must verify the signature with the correct secret or public key, which is what the optional verify section does. Treat a decoded payload as untrusted until it is verified.

faq.q: Which algorithms can this tool verify, and how?
faq.a: Verification runs in your browser with the Web Crypto API. For HS256, HS384 and HS512 you supply the shared secret (plain text, or tick the box if it is base64). For RS256/384/512 and ES256/384 you supply the public key as PEM (an SPKI 'BEGIN PUBLIC KEY' block) or as JWK JSON. The tool recomputes the signature over header.payload and reports Verified or Invalid signature. Changing even one character of the payload makes a valid signature fail.

faq.q: Why does a token with five parts say it cannot be decoded?
faq.a: A five-part token is a JWE (JSON Web Encryption), not a JWS. Its payload is encrypted, so unlike a normal signed JWT it cannot be read by decoding alone — only someone with the decryption key can see the contents. The tool detects the five-part structure and tells you this rather than printing garbage. A normal readable JWT has exactly three parts.

faq.q: Why do non-ASCII claims like Hindi names display correctly here?
faq.a: The Base64URL payload is decoded to raw bytes and then run through a UTF-8 TextDecoder, so multi-byte characters are reconstructed properly. A naive atob() alone would mangle them. That means a claim such as "नाम":"अंकित" shows its real characters. The tool also fixes Base64URL padding and translates the URL-safe characters before decoding, and reports a clear message instead of crashing on malformed input.
